positions.commentary: The speaker compares Coca-Cola's valuation in 1998 to its performance 13 years later, noting that while business and net income doubled, market cap shrank.
The speaker notes that Microsoft was a great business but the stock was too expensive in 1999, resulting in zero returns over 16 years despite revenue growth.

thesis: This episode argues that while Microsoft and Coca-Cola were great businesses, their stocks were too expensive in 1999 and 1998 respectively, leading to poor returns over the following decade. The speaker emphasizes that bottling businesses with partners like Coca-Cola, Pepsi, or Varun Beverages offer superior returns due to symbiotic relationships and strong governance, particularly highlighting growth in markets like Pakistan, Russia, and Turkey.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Microsoft was a great business but the stock was too expensive in 1999, resulting in zero returns over 16 years despite revenue growth.
claims.quote: And if you look at the, you look at the Microsoft chart from 99 to 2015, including all the reinvested dividends, the return was zero. And it's a great business. It's been a great business throughout that time, you know, but it was just too expensive.

claims.claim: The speaker describes the relationship between Coca-Cola and its bottlers as symbiotic, where Coke sets up brands for the benefit of the bottler, which also benefits Coke.
claims.quote: So all that branding is done by the Coca-Cola company for the benefit of the bottler, which also benefits the Coca-Cola company. So it's a symbiotic relationship.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that bottling businesses can be really good because both Coke and Pepsi want the bottlers to do well and set them up to do well.
claims.quote: But the bottling business can be a really good business because basically both these companies want the bottlers to do well, and they set up the bottles to do well.

claims.claim: The speaker states that a bottling business with Coke or Pepsi as a partner is vastly superior with much higher returns on capital.
claims.quote: And when you have a bottling business with Coke or Pepsi as a bottler as a partner, clearly the Coke and pepper, Bepsy business is vastly superior, you know, much higher returns on capital.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that in Pakistan, the case volume for a bottler grew from 40 million cases to 400 million cases in 15 years despite the country having problems.
claims.quote: So like, for example, in Pakistan, the case volume, 15 years ago, the unit case volume that Kukala Isaac had was about 40 million cases. cases a year 15 years ago. Now it is 400 million cases. And it's 400 million cases in a basket case country with a lot of problems.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights that Coke Studio Pakistan was enormously successful and completely paid for by the Coca-Cola company, not the bottler.
claims.quote: So Coke Studio, Pakistan, for example, is completely paid for by the Coca-Cola company. It's not paid by the bottler. So all that branding is done by the Coca-Cola company for the benefit of the bottler, which also benefits the Coca-Cola company.

claims.claim: The speaker compares Coca-Cola's valuation in 1998 to its performance 13 years later, noting that while business and net income doubled, market cap shrank.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Varun Beverages is an exceptional business with incredible tailwinds in India, projecting significant growth in volume and market cap over the next 10-15 years.
claims.quote: And one is based in India, Varun beverages, which I'm sure most of you are familiar with. And the other one, Coca-Cola, Isoc, is based in Turkey. But they do bottling in about a dozen countries.

claims.claim: The speaker projects Varun Beverages could grow to a 19-25 billion market cap based on volume growth assumptions, representing a 1.3 to 3.3% annualized return plus dividends.
claims.quote: And if those were the growth numbers, basically, you would have about five times the volume that you have today. and a quarter billion of after-tax earnings growing at a bit, about 8%, maybe you would give it a 15-20 multiple, 19 to 25 billion market cap.
